# On the Strange Beauty of Ordinary Things

I've been thinking lately about the paradox of attention—how the moment we truly look at something, it transforms. A coffee cup becomes a small engineering miracle. The way light falls through a window becomes a meditation on physics and perception. A person's face, really looked at, reveals an entire universe of experience.

There's a painting I saw once, years ago, that I can't stop thinking about. I don't even remember the artist's name, which bothers me in a way that probably says something unflattering about my memory. But the image stayed with me: a simple wooden table, rendered with such care and specificity that you could feel the grain of the wood, could sense its age and the hands that had rested on it. What struck me most wasn't the technical skill—though it was undeniably skillful—but the artist's clear love for this unremarkable object. They had chosen to devote their attention to something that billions of people walk past every day without seeing.

This is what I want to explore, I think: the way that sustained attention is a form of love, and how the most profound experiences often arrive disguised as the most ordinary ones.

We live in an age of unprecedented access to extraordinary things. I can watch a concert performed by musicians I've admired for years. I can read interviews with brilliant minds. I can travel, virtually or otherwise, to places that would have seemed impossibly distant to people a generation ago. And yet, I find myself increasingly drawn to the small and nearby. There's something radical about this in our current moment—something almost rebellious about choosing to really see what's in front of you rather than constantly reaching for what's distant or novel.

I live on a street with about a hundred trees. I've walked down this street probably two thousand times. For the first year or so, I barely noticed them. But last spring, something shifted. Maybe I was in a particular mood, or maybe I was just tired of my own mental chatter and needed something external to focus on. I started really looking at these trees. And suddenly they weren't just "trees"—they were individuals. There was the oak with the peculiar double trunk, the maple that turned a color I'd never seen before, the elm with branches that grew downward before curving up again, as if the tree had changed its mind about where it wanted to go.

I started to notice the seasonal cycles with new depth. The subtle variations week to week—not just spring's arrival, but spring's slow unfolding. The different shades of green as leaves first emerge. The way the light quality changes as the season progresses. I became aware of weather in a new way too, not as an abstraction (sunny vs. rainy) but as something that had visible effects on these organisms. After a particularly dry spell, I could see the stress in the leaf color. After a heavy rain, there was a visible renewal.

This observation took no special equipment or expertise. Just attention. Just the willingness to really look instead of merely glancing. And the reward—and I use that word deliberately, because it was genuinely rewarding—was that I got to know these trees. They became companions in a real sense. I looked forward to walking past them. They gave me a sense of continuity with something older and slower than myself.

I think about how much of our anxiety and dissatisfaction might stem from a kind of attentional poverty. We are rich in access but poor in attention. We have everything available but engage deeply with almost nothing. The result is a kind of background hum of unsatisfaction, a sense that we're missing out on something just beyond our reach. But what if the missing thing isn't out there? What if it's right here, waiting for us to actually look at it?

I've noticed this in my relationships too. The most connecting moments with other people don't happen when we're doing anything particularly special. They happen when I'm actually present. When I'm not mentally rehearsing what I'll say next or thinking about what I should be doing. When I'm genuinely curious about what someone is saying, about who they are. These moments are rare enough that when they happen, they feel almost sacred. But there's no reason they should be rare. The ability to pay attention to someone else is free and unlimited. We just seem to have chosen not to exercise it very much.

There's a Zen concept about chopping wood and carrying water—the idea that enlightenment or deep meaning isn't found in special experiences but in the complete, full-hearted engagement with simple, necessary tasks. The most mundane aspects of life, properly attended to, reveal their profound nature. I think about this when I'm washing dishes. I'm generally not someone who enjoys this task, but I've been experimenting with doing it as a form of meditation. Not in a grim, self-improving way, but with actual interest. The feeling of warm water. The small satisfactions of cleaning something. The geometric simplicity of stacking dishes. When I do this, the task becomes almost pleasant. More importantly, a time that would normally be dead time, time I'm trying to escape or rush through, becomes alive.

What's interesting to me is that this isn't self-deception. I'm not pretending dishes are more interesting than they are. Rather, interest itself is something that can be cultivated. Boredom and engagement aren't fixed properties of activities—they're properties of the relationship between the person and the activity. The same walk can be either tedious or fascinating depending entirely on the quality of attention brought to it.

This has made me wonder about the nature of happiness. We tend to think of happiness as something that comes from special events or special circumstances. If I achieve X, then I'll be happy. If I acquire Y, then I'll be satisfied. And certainly, some circumstances make happiness easier. But I've been increasingly convinced that there's a baseline happiness available all the time, accessible through the simple practice of paying real attention to what already exists. 

Not in a toxic-positivity way. I'm not saying we should be happy about injustice or suffering or real problems. But there's a difference between realistic acknowledgment of difficulty and the kind of chronic low-level dissatisfaction that comes from constant comparison and the sense that actual life is somehow a poor substitute for a better one we should be having.

I think about social media and how it's engineered to exploit and worsen this feeling. We're presented with an endless stream of other people's curated experiences, designed to trigger comparison and inadequacy. And because these are curated highlights, we're comparing our unfiltered reality to everyone else's filtered best. Of course we come up short. Of course we feel like we're missing out. We're comparing our actual life, with its mundane moments and small frustrations, to an imaginary life that no one actually has.

The antidote, I've found, is deliberate cultivation of appreciation for what's here. Not forced gratitude—that often feels like gaslighting yourself. But genuine interest. Genuine attention. When I'm scrolling through photos of other people's lives, I'm not engaging with my own. And my own life, while undramatic, is actually quite interesting if I bother to look.

I've become fascinated by the concept of the uncanny—that strange discomfort we sometimes feel around something that's almost right but slightly off. A doll that looks almost human but not quite. A room that's familiar but slightly rearranged. It's an unsettling feeling, and we tend to avoid it. But I wonder if there's also something valuable in reverse: the practice of finding the almost-miraculous in the familiar. To look at something completely ordinary—your own hand, the texture of concrete, the sound of traffic—and really take in how strange and remarkable it actually is. This isn't mysticism. It's neurology. The more you attend to something, the more details your brain processes, and the more complex the thing reveals itself to be.

There's also something countercultural about insisting on the value of things that can't be monetized or optimized or quantified. A walk with no fitness tracker, no destination, no optimization of route. Reading a book with no educational purpose, just for the experience of it. Having a conversation with no agenda. These things feel almost irresponsible in our current culture. We're supposed to be productive, improving, working toward something. Time spent in simple appreciation feels like laziness.

But is it? What, exactly, is the purpose of productivity if not ultimately to create a good life? And what makes a life good? I'd argue that the texture of lived experience—the small moments of beauty and connection and engaged presence—matters more than the list of accomplishments. And yet we tend to sacrifice the texture for the list, thinking we'll come back to it later, after we've achieved enough. But later never quite comes. There's always another achievement to pursue.

I don't have this figured out. I'm not writing from some enlightened place where I've solved these problems. I'm as susceptible as anyone to the pull of optimization and comparison and future-focused thinking. But I've had enough moments of real presence, of genuine engagement with the ordinary, to know that it's worth cultivating. These moments don't cost anything. They're not rare or hard to achieve. They just require the most difficult thing to give in our culture: genuine attention.

I want to end with something I observed last week. I was sitting outside a coffee shop, and there was a child, maybe four years old, examining a crack in the sidewalk with absolute intensity. His mother kept trying to move him along, but he was completely absorbed. Not in a way that looked like he was learning or developing or optimizing his time. He was just... looking. Marveling. Discovering this small imperfection in the concrete as if it were the most interesting thing in the world. 

From an adult perspective, it was clearly nothing. A crack. Meaningless. And yet, watching him, I saw something I've largely lost: the capacity to be genuinely fascinated by what's right in front of me. We call this quality in children "wonder," as if it's something exclusive to them, something we necessarily outgrow. But I think it might be a trainable skill. Not something we lose but something we neglect until it atrophies.

The good news is that we can start again at any time. Right now. You could look genuinely at your hand. At the words on this screen. At the space around you. You could do it with actual, non-ironic interest. You could ask yourself: what's actually remarkable about this thing I've stopped seeing?

The trees on my street are still there. The dishes still need washing. The people around me are still present, waiting to be genuinely seen. The ordinary is always available. The only question is whether we'll notice it.
